A decomposition is a rewrite $A = \cdots$ that makes a computation,
or a geometric fact, cheap. Before the factorisations, the objects
being multiplied have to be named. The galleries below are from
[@eeanimation](https://www.instagram.com/eeanimation/).

## Introduction to vectors {#sec-vectors}

A vector is an element of a vector space: you can add two and scale
one, and you stay in the space. Arrows in the plane are the first
picture, not the definition. Functions, polynomials, and matrices
can be vectors too.

## Vector multiplications {#sec-products}

There is no single “times” for vectors. The symbol decides the
output: a scalar (dot), a perpendicular vector (cross), a matrix
(outer), a bivector (wedge), or a multivector (geometric product).

[14 September 2026](https://www.instagram.com/p/DdRMj3FjIGR/).

## Methods of matrix inversion {#sec-inverse}

There is no single best inverse. Gauss–Jordan is pedagogical;
adjugate is for small symbolic work; LU, QR, Cholesky, and SVD are
the numerical defaults. Forming $A^{-1}$ is often the wrong move:
solve $Ax=b$ with a factorisation instead.

[4 September 2026](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dc3ckPsD-uA/).

## Eigenvalue algorithms {#sec-eigen}

$A v = \lambda v$ is the decomposition $A = X\Lambda X^{-1}$ when $A$
is diagonalisable. Which *algorithm* you want depends on whether $A$
is sparse or symmetric, and on whether you need one eigenpair or the
whole spectrum. Do not form $\det(A-\lambda I)$ as a numerical
primitive.

[6 September 2026](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dc8mHiMj7og/).

## Factorisations by job {#sec-table}

| Decomposition | Shape / hypotheses | Typical use |
|---------------|--------------------|-------------|
| LU (with pivoting) | Square, generic | Solve $Ax=b$; determinant |
| QR | Full column rank | Least squares; orthonormal bases |
| Cholesky | Hermitian positive definite | Fast $Ax=b$; covariance |
| Eigen $A = X\Lambda X^{-1}$ | Square, diagonalisable | Powers, linear ODEs $\dot x = Ax$ |
| Spectral $A = Q\Lambda Q^\top$ | Symmetric / Hermitian | Axes of a quadratic form |
| SVD $A = U\Sigma V^\top$ | Any | Rank, condition, PCA, low-rank approx. |
| Polar | Square, invertible | Closest rotation times stretch |
| Schur | Square | Numerically stable “eigen” form |
| Jordan | Square, over $\mathbb C$ | Theoretical canonical form (unstable) |

After you linearise a vector field
([differential equations](../dynamics/differential-equations.qmd)),
the local picture is $\dot x = Ax$. The eigen- or Schur form of $A$
is the dynamical classification.
